c.tagline: Ancient southern capital of dynasties, city walls, and Yangtze lore.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares start around 11 CNY; most locals hail via Didi. Foreign credit cards are rarely accepted, so pay by Alipay/WeChat or cash.

emergency.note: Police is 110, ambulance/medical is 120, and fire is 119. English-speaking operators are limited, so having your address in Chinese helps.

avoid.reason: Around the Confucius Temple (Fuzimiao) and other tourist areas, decline 'tea ceremony' or 'art student' invitations, which are overcharging scams.

hood_desc: Nanjing's downtown core and one of China's busiest commercial hubs, centered on the Xinjiekou traffic circle and Zifeng Tower; packed with malls, department stores, offices, and metro interchanges, it is the most convenient walkable base for first-timers.

The historic soul of Nanjing along the Qinhuai River, home to the Confucius Temple (Fuzimiao), the Imperial Examination Museum, and lantern-lit night markets; touristy but atmospheric, best for sightseeing and evening strolls by the water.

A green, relaxed district wrapped around Xuanwu Lake and the Ming-era city wall, with parks, lakeside promenades, and Jiming Temple nearby; suits travelers wanting calm scenery and open space near the center.

The forested Purple Mountain (Zhongshan) scenic area on the eastern edge of the city, holding the Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum, the Ming Xiaoling Tomb, and Linggu Temple; a sights-and-nature retreat of trails, gardens, and monuments.

Hexi is Nanjing's modern riverfront new town in Jianye District, built around the Youth Olympic Sports Park, the Nanjing International Expo Center, and Hexi CBD skyscrapers; orderly, spacious, and business-oriented.

water.note: Stick to bottled or boiled water; avoid tap water and ice made from it.

transit.hours: Metro trains generally run from around 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM; buses run roughly 5:30 AM to 11:00 PM, with taxis and Didi filling the late-night gap.
transit.note: Nanjing Metro is one of China's largest systems with a dozen lines linking the airport, both high-speed rail stations, and most sights; it is the fastest and cheapest way around, backed by an extensive bus network.
transit.pay: Pay by QR code through Alipay, WeChat, or the Nanjing Metro app; a rechargeable Jinlingtong transit card and single-journey tokens are also sold at station machines. Fares are distance-based, starting around 2 CNY.

bus: Intercity coaches from Nanjing Bus Terminals to regional cities

car.idp: Required (foreign licenses not valid; a temporary Chinese permit is needed)

ferry: Yangtze River local ferry crossings (e.g. Zhongshan Wharf)
train: Nanjing South Railway Station (major high-speed rail hub)

transit.m: Metro Line S1 (Airport Line) to city center via Nanjing South (~35-45 min)
Airport coach to city center (~45-60 min)
Taxi to city center (50-60 min, ~130-150 CNY)

tip.r: Tipping is not customary or expected in Nanjing; restaurants, taxis, and cafes do not anticipate a tip, though upscale hotels may add a service charge.

food.name: Nanjing Salted Duck (Yanshui Ya)
food.desc: The city's emblem - duck dry-cured, gently poached and chilled, giving pale, juicy meat with a clean saltiness. Sold by weight to eat in or take away.

places.name: Han Fu Xing
places.note: Century-old salted duck house, the name locals give when asked where to buy it.

places.name: Ma Xiang Xing
places.note: Historic halal restaurant famous for its classic Nanjing duck dishes and banquet cooking.

places.name: Confucius Temple Snack Street
places.note: Dozens of counters sell vacuum-packed salted duck by the half, handy for taking away.

food.name: Duck Blood and Vermicelli Soup
food.desc: Nanjing's everyday bowl: sweet potato vermicelli in duck broth with duck blood curd, liver, gizzard and tofu puffs, finished with chili oil and coriander.

places.name: Yong He Yuan
places.note: Old-brand Nanjing snack house; its duck blood soup is the benchmark version.

places.name: Huiwei Duck Blood Vermicelli Soup
places.note: Reliable Nanjing-born chain, consistent bowls and picture menus for visitors.

places.name: Ya De Bao
places.note: Duck-soup specialist with the most branches; good late-night fallback.

food.name: Chicken Broth Tangbao
food.desc: Steamed soup dumplings filled with pork and chicken-broth jelly, eaten through a straw or nibbled at the top - a Nanjing breakfast institution.

places.name: Yin Shi Tangbao
places.note: The Nanjing name for chicken-broth soup dumplings; cheap and always busy at breakfast.

places.name: Yong He Yuan
places.note: Old-brand teahouse pairing tangbao with the classic Qinhuai snack set.

places.name: Kuiguang Ge
places.note: Long-standing Confucius Temple snack hall serving the eight famous Qinhuai snacks.

food.name: Pidu Noodles (Pork Skin Noodles)
food.desc: Wide alkaline noodles in a pork-bone broth with puffed fried pork skin, pork liver, meatballs and greens - the city's most-loved cheap lunch.

places.name: Xiang Ji Noodle House
places.note: Long-running pidu mian shop locals queue at; order it with everything in the bowl.

places.name: Lan Laoda Noodles
places.note: Veteran pidu noodle specialist near the universities, generous toppings.

places.name: Liu Chang Xing
places.note: Century-old noodle and pastry brand, a safe central choice for pidu noodles.

food.name: Duck Oil Sesame Shaobing
food.desc: Flaky sesame-crusted flatbread enriched with rendered duck fat, sold hot from the oven and eaten as a snack or alongside duck blood soup.

places.name: Liu Chang Xing
places.note: Old-brand bakery counter turning out duck oil shaobing straight from the oven.

places.name: Yong He Yuan
places.note: Serves the shaobing as part of the traditional Qinhuai snack lineup.

places.name: Confucius Temple Snack Street
places.note: Several stalls bake shaobing to order; look for the ones with a queue.

food.name: Beef Pot Stickers and Beef Soup
food.desc: Nanjing's halal snack pairing - crisp-bottomed beef dumplings fried in long rows, served with a clear peppery beef and vermicelli soup.

places.name: Li Ji Halal Restaurant
places.note: Famous Muslim snack shop known citywide for beef pot stickers and beef soup.

places.name: Ma Xiang Xing
places.note: Historic halal kitchen; a sit-down option for beef dishes away from the crowds.

places.name: Confucius Temple Snack Street
places.note: Halal counters along the lane fry pot stickers continuously through the day.

food.name: Yuhua Tea
food.desc: Nanjing's own green tea, rolled into dark pine-needle shapes and grown on the hills south of the city - light, grassy and slightly sweet.

places.name: Confucius Temple Teahouses
places.note: Canal-side teahouses serve Yuhua tea by the pot with Qinhuai snacks.

places.name: Yong He Yuan
places.note: Traditional snack house where tea comes with the classic snack platter.

places.name: Zhonghua Gate Tea Shops
places.note: Tea merchants near the old city wall sell and brew loose Yuhua leaf.

food.name: Osmanthus Wine (Guihua Jiu)
food.desc: Sweet golden wine perfumed with osmanthus blossom, a Nanjing autumn tradition when the city's sweet-olive trees flower.

places.name: Confucius Temple Snack Street
places.note: Shops sell bottled osmanthus wine and osmanthus sour-plum drinks to go.

places.name: Ma Xiang Xing
places.note: Classic Nanjing banquet restaurant; osmanthus wine suits the sweet-savory dishes.

places.name: Lao Men Dong Lanes
places.note: Restored old-quarter lanes full of small bars pouring osmanthus and rice wines.

landmarks: Sun Yat-sen Mausoleum
A monumental granite and blue-tiled memorial climbing the slopes of Purple Mountain, honoring the father of modern China with sweeping panoramic views.
Nanjing City Wall (Zhonghua Gate)
The best-preserved and longest ancient city wall in China, with the massive Zhonghua Gate fortress showcasing 600-year-old Ming dynasty defenses.
Presidential Palace
A sprawling historic complex that served as the seat of power for the Taiping Kingdom and Republic of China, rich with classical Chinese and Western-style architecture.
Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall
A powerful and moving memorial complex commemorating the 1937 tragedy, essential for understanding the city's modern history.
Confucius Temple (Fuzimiao)
A bustling riverside temple district with glowing lanterns, ornate gateways, and boat rides along the Qinhuai River, especially magical at night.
Xuanwu Lake
A vast scenic lake dotted with islands and pagodas right next to the city wall, offering some of Nanjing's most tranquil skyline reflections.
Nanjing Museum
One of China's oldest and largest museums, housing imperial treasures and stunning architecture that blends ancient and contemporary design.
Nanjing Yangtze River Bridge
An engineering landmark of the Mao era, its monumental socialist-realist statues and sweeping double-deck span remain a proud symbol of the city.
Jiming Temple
A vividly colored hillside Buddhist temple near Xuanwu Lake, famous for its cherry blossoms in spring and vibrant multi-tiered pagoda.
Purple Mountain (Zijin Shan)
A forested mountain overlooking the city, home to numerous historic sites and offering the best panoramic views and hiking trails in Nanjing.

train.note: Nanjing has no international trains, but it is one of the busiest high-speed junctions in China. Nanjing South handles most high-speed departures, with Shanghai about 75 minutes away, Beijing about 4 hours, Hefei around an hour and Wuhan 3.5-4 hours, while the older Nanjing Station on the north side of the city keeps conventional and some high-speed services. Both stations are on the metro, which makes transfers straightforward, and Nanjing North serves nearby Yangzhou, Zhenjiang and Suzhou traffic. Book on 12306 with your passport - Shanghai-Nanjing trains run every few minutes and rarely sell out entirely.

bus.note: There are no international coach services from Nanjing. Most long-distance buses leave from Zhongyangmen bus station, about ten minutes west of the main train station, with regular runs to Shanghai, Hangzhou and destinations across Jiangsu and Anhui, plus Beijing in around 12 hours and an overnight sleeper to Guangzhou in about 24 hours. Additional terminals operate at Nanjing South (Zhonghuamen), Hanzhongmen and Nanjing East. For anywhere on the high-speed network the train is dramatically quicker, so the coach is mainly for small county towns.

ferry.note: Nanjing is a river port on the Yangtze, but the scheduled long-distance passenger liners that once linked it with Shanghai and Wuhan no longer operate, and the cruise ships that call at Nanjing are round-trip sightseeing vessels rather than point-to-point transport. The only regular boats are the short cross-river ferries, notably from Zhongshan Wharf over to Pukou on the north bank, which take a few minutes and are used as local commuter transport.

half.name: Yangzhou
half.blurb: A canal city on the Grand Canal with classical gardens, including the Slender West Lake park.

half.name: Zhenjiang
half.blurb: A Yangtze River city with the hilltop Jinshan and Jiaoshan temple complexes rising from the water.

half.name: Suzhou
half.blurb: A canal city known for its UNESCO-listed classical gardens, including the Humble Administrator's Garden.
